courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer
md: Tagged pointer = pointer plus a counter compared and swapped as one unit, bumped on every successful CAS. It turns "same value" into "same value and same version".

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals
md: Queries are not the only noise source. If a stage is trained, its score also varies with the random seed. Use the same seeds and checkpoints for every stage you are not ablating, and when the ablated stage itself is retrained, run several seeds and report the spread, or a seed-to-seed swing can masquerade as a component effect.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: tau-bench: simulated users, database state and pass^k
md: pass@k rewards finding a solution in k tries (useful when a verifier can pick the winner). pass^k rewards solving it every time (what a deployed agent needs). For independent trials with success p they are $1-(1-p)^k$ and $p^k$; across tasks, pass^k depends heavily on how p is spread.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Why an agent cannot just replay its whole history
md: Misconception: a memory layer makes the agent remember *better* than full history. On LoCoMo, where a conversation still fits in the window, full context scored highest in the Mem0 paper. Memory wins when history no longer fits, or when the cost and latency of re-reading it every turn are unacceptable.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Layer the checks: deterministic first, judges last
md: The multiplication assumes independent errors, which is optimistic. A judge and a test suite written from the same misunderstanding of the spec fail on the same wrong answers, so the real chain FPR is higher than the product.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: A crystal as data: lattice, fractional coordinates, periodicity
md: A crystal is a set of atom types, fractional coordinates in [0, 1), and a 3x3 lattice. Cartesian position is $f$ times $L$, coordinates wrap mod 1, and every distance must use the minimum image.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: The soft watermark: add delta to the green logits
md: $\delta$ trades watermark strength against quality; $\gamma$ sets how often human text hits green by chance. The detector depends only on $\gamma$ and the hash rule, never on $\delta$, so a provider can change $\delta$ per product without changing the detector.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
md: Replay is open-loop: the program's computation between calls is gone, so cache contents and timing differ, and cycles per call in replay are not the application's allocator time. Use replay for memory comparisons and relative call costs, and confirm with a real run.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Anomalies in time: seasonal baselines and robust residuals
md: Anomalies in the history contaminate the baseline. If last Tuesday's outage is in the training window, a mean-based baseline and standard deviation absorb it and become blind to the next one. That is why both the toy baseline here and S-H-ESD use medians and MAD: one bad day out of 27 does not move a same-hour median.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
md: ARIES in one line: **repeat history, then undo the losers, logging every undo as a redo-only CLR whose UndoNextLSN skips what is already undone**. That makes recovery idempotent: crash during analysis or redo and you simply start over; crash during undo and you resume where the CLRs say.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
md: `gather` does not cancel siblings on failure. With the default `return_exceptions=False`, the first exception propagates to the caller but the docs state the other awaitables "won't be cancelled and will continue to run". If you want per-item errors without losing the batch, pass `return_exceptions=True` and inspect each result; if one failure should stop everything, use a `TaskGroup`.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Inside Tokio's scheduler: local queues, stealing, LIFO slot
md: Tokio guarantees fairness only in a weak sense: if the number of tasks is bounded and no task blocks, every woken task is eventually scheduled. It does **not** promise round-robin order. Two ready tasks A and B may see A scheduled five times before B, even if A calls `yield_now`.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: Clip length does not map to patches by simple division. YAMNet needs at least 0.975 s of audio (0.96 s plus the rest of the last 25 ms STFT window), pads anything shorter with silence, and rounds longer audio up to a whole hop. Our script gets 1 patch for 0.5 s, **2 patches for 1.0 s**, 10 for 5 s and 20 for 10 s.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tokens, budgets and when to stop
md: Tokens buy research quality (80% of BrowseComp variance in Anthropic's analysis), so the budget is the main dial. Enforce budgets in the harness, reserve a share for synthesis and verification, and scale effort to the question.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Customizing models: fine-tuning, distillation, pretraining and import
md: Serving rules for custom models have changed over time. A 2023 AWS launch post said custom models needed Provisioned Throughput; current docs also offer on-demand custom model deployments, but only for listed base models and Regions. Check the current page before you promise a serving cost.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: A correctly predicted branch is nearly free. A mispredicted one costs about as many cycles as the pipeline is deep. Agner Fog gives roughly 0 to 2 cycles for a predicted branch and about 15 to 25 cycles for a misprediction on modern x86 cores.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: B+trees update in place, and random writes pay for it
md: A B+tree's write cost is set by the **page**, not the row: a random small update rewrites a whole page at a random location. Reads are cheap because each key lives in exactly one place.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: The buffer pool: frames, a page table, pins and dirty pages
md: A buffer pool is a write-back page cache owned by the database. On a miss it must evict some *unpinned* page, and write it out first if it is *dirty*. Everything else in this course is about choosing that page well.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Entropy patching: spend compute where the next byte is hard
md: Entropy depends on context, which can backfire. On a few-shot MMLU prompt, repeated phrases became very predictable, so they were swallowed into huge patches (the paper calls this entropy drift). The fix for the large run: reset the entropy model's context at newlines and use the monotonic rule.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker
md: `unsafe` does not change the rules; it changes who checks them. Rust programs must never cause undefined behavior, inside or outside unsafe blocks. Inside, the proof obligation moves from the compiler to you.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Power-of-two strides are a trap. In this L1d every address 4096 bytes apart maps to the same set, and a set has only 8 ways. Walking a column of `double m[N][512]` (rows of exactly 4 KB) puts every line in one set: only 8 of them can be cached at once even though the cache holds 512 lines.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Validating a graph with interventions
md: Graph first, intervention second. The graph proposes which features matter and how; perturbing those features in the real model is what turns a picture into evidence. Expect directional agreement, not exact numbers.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: Pick the propensity source by how much user disruption you can afford: randomization or swaps are simplest and most trustworthy, EM and intervention harvesting use existing logs but rest on model assumptions, and DLA learns everything jointly. Every option inherits the click model's assumptions; if users behave like a cascade, a position-only propensity is misspecified.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Three things the silhouette cannot do. It is undefined for k = 1, so it can never tell you "this data has no clusters" (our k = 3 winner at 0.54 is not strong evidence of anything). It needs all pairwise distances, so it costs O(n squared) work. And it rewards compact well-separated blobs, so it is biased toward the kind of answer k-means produces, which makes it a poor referee between k-means and a density method.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
md: A selection vector is not a filtered copy. Downstream primitives read the original vectors at the listed positions. That avoids copying, but the reads are now indirect and sparse, which matters for SIMD (next lesson).

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
md: LTO can expose latent bugs. Code with undefined behavior, or with mismatched declarations of the same function in different files, may have "worked" only because the optimizer could not see across files. When LTO breaks a program, suspect the program first.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Why long tasks fail: compounding errors and verification
md: Task success is roughly a product of step successes, so long tasks need both a high per-step rate and a check after each step that actually detects failure. Check the resulting state, not just whether an action ran.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
md: TSan reports races that **did not cause a failure** in this run. It needs only that both conflicting accesses execute and that nothing orders them by happens-before. That is its big advantage over stress testing.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: What a consistency model promises, and why replicas break it
md: Model A is **stronger** than model B when every history A allows is also allowed by B (A is a subset of B). Stronger models rule out more surprising results, and usually cost more coordination, latency or availability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
md: Consistent hashing minimises *movement*. It does not by itself give *balance*. With one random token per node, arcs vary wildly in size, as the toy ring shows. The next lesson fixes that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Too few results: relaxation ladders and post-hoc constraints
md: Three layers, three tools: per-document requirements are **filters**, per-document preferences are a **weighted score**, and requirements on the list as a whole are a **re-ranking pass**. When filters starve the list, relax in a declared order, keep the non-negotiables hard, and say what you relaxed.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
md: A solver turns a declarative model into search plus propagation plus learning. Your job is the model: tight domains, global constraints instead of many small ones, integer scaling, and a time limit with a status check.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Do reasoning models admit the hints they use?
md: When the model can act on information without reasoning about it, its CoT usually stays silent about it, even with no pressure to hide. CoT monitoring then helps you notice frequent behaviors, but it cannot certify that a behavior is absent.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A cross-encoder is not a better embedding model. It has no vector output you could store in a vector database. If someone asks you to index a corpus with a reranker, the answer is that you cannot: the score exists only for a specific query.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Intensity per tile is not the whole story. Two CTAs that share a row of tiles both read the same slice of A, and the L2 cache may serve the second read. CUTLASS's threadblock rasterization (swizzling the CTA launch order) exists to make that L2 reuse more likely.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: Fast CUTLASS kernels come from a few choices: tile shape (reuse versus occupancy and wave fit), stage count (latency hiding versus shared memory), kernel schedule (cooperative or ping-pong) and the epilogue fusion. CuTe layouts make each choice a type parameter instead of a rewrite.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
md: CXL makes memory placement a policy problem again. The hardware gives you a slower, bigger NUMA tier; the operating system (tiering) or the cluster manager (pooling) must keep hot data local and push only cold or untouched data to it.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: SoA is not automatically faster. Its advantage is exactly the fraction of each record that a loop does *not* touch. A loop that uses every field gains nothing from the layout change, and some access patterns get worse (lesson 2).

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
md: Floating-point addition is commutative but not associative. Reordering a sum is not a refactor, it is a different computation. Every other idea in this course follows from that sentence.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
md: A diffusion language model keeps the Transformer and the maximum-likelihood goal of a GPT. It changes two things: attention is bidirectional, and generation fills in many masked positions per step in any order instead of one token at the end.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
md: Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets TPOT. Putting both in one batch makes each phase pay for the other.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob
md: A common misreading: larger alpha prunes *more*. It is the opposite. The removal test gets harder to pass as alpha grows, so more candidates survive, the average degree rises (up to the cap R), and search paths get shorter. The cost is memory and more distance computations per hop.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: KTO keeps DPO's implicit reward and reference model but drops pairing: each example is scored against a shared reference point (the estimated KL drift) instead of against a sibling answer. That lets it train on binary feedback, and on imbalanced data via $\lambda_D, \lambda_U$.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Scientist is for code that only reads. Its README says that because the candidate may or may not run, it is only safe for wrapping methods that do not change data. Write paths need different checks, such as comparing stored rows after the fact.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
md: The verifier runs once, at load time, and proves properties of **all** paths: bounded execution, typed pointers, null checks before dereference, initialized registers, in-bounds stack and map access. Because the proof is done up front, the JIT-compiled code needs no runtime checks and runs at native speed.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
md: Plain SFT on short samples barely helped here (a 2.0% cut on MATH500). Imitating short traces is weaker than contrasting short against long, because the model never sees what it should move away from.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: NILM is an inverse problem: one observed sum, many hidden parts. Every algorithm you will meet differs only in what extra knowledge it uses to choose among the many decompositions that add up to the same total.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match
md: A pair that blocking drops is classified as a non-match without ever being looked at. No scoring model can recover it. Use several strict rules joined by OR (Splink's advice: a longer list of strict rules beats a short list of loose ones), so a typo in one field is caught by a rule on another.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Inside epoll: interest list, ready list, epoll_wait
md: epoll cannot help with disk files. `epoll_ctl` fails with `EPERM` for a regular file or directory, and poll reports such files as always ready, because a disk read never becomes "ready" in advance: it just has to wait for the device. Event loops send file I/O to a thread pool (next lessons) or use io_uring.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
md: Hold out queries, not pairs, and cluster near-duplicates before splitting. Tune on dev as much as you like, read the sealed test set rarely and for decisions you declared in advance, and replace it on a schedule.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
md: False sharing needs three things at once: two or more cores, one cache line, and at least one writer. Remove any one (single thread, separate lines, or read-only data) and the line stops bouncing.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
md: Simplified model: ours is one parameter, convex, deterministic, full-batch and fully participating. Real drift in a deep network is worse and messier (it interacts with batch normalization statistics, momentum and client sampling), but the direction of the error is the one computed here.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
md: Separate two numbers for every MoE model: **total parameters** (all experts, what you store) and **activated parameters** (what one token actually uses, which sets FLOPs per token). DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total and 37B activated per token.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, scheduling, and using the kernels
md: Each generation chases the bottleneck the previous hardware exposed. FlashAttention removed HBM traffic for $S$ and $P$. FlashAttention-2 fixed work partitioning. FlashAttention-3 used Hopper's asynchrony to hide softmax and loads under the matmuls. FlashAttention-4 attacks the exponential unit and shared memory bandwidth, which stopped scaling with Blackwell's tensor cores.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Crossing lines and why the learned paths curve
md: Straight training targets do not mean straight sampling paths. Each conditional path is a line, but the marginal flow, which is what the network learns and what sampling follows, curves wherever many lines cross.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: "FP8 training" does not mean every tensor is FP8. In the FP8 paper, DeepSeek-V3 and the NVFP4 report alike, only the *inputs* to GEMMs are FP8. GEMM outputs come out in BF16 or FP32, and normalizations, softmax, the master weights and optimizer state stay in higher precision.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: The write-ahead rule: flush the log first, pages later
md: The write-ahead rule, in PostgreSQL's words: changes to data files must be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. A commit is durable once its commit record is flushed; data pages can be written much later.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees
md: Both indexes trade exactness of the first step for speed: a trigram index proposes candidates by a cheap overlap count, a BK-tree rules out subtrees with the triangle inequality. Neither changes the final score; you still verify candidates with the metric you trust.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion
md: Retrieval is cheap and noisy; verification is strict. Each match is a full alignment that predicts many other stars, and the Bayes factor multiplies independent evidence, so a true match passes 1e9 within a handful of stars while chance matches almost never do.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Pixels in memory: NHWC, NCHW, pitch and a warp's 96 bytes
md: For a per-pixel operator, layout plus pitch decides how wide an aligned access each lane can make. NHWC gives a pixel's channels locality and lets one load carry a whole pixel when channels are padded to 4; NCHW gives each channel a unit-stride stream. Neither is wrong, and both lose if the kernel accesses one byte at a time.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Best fit, splitting and merging inside segments
md: Best fit plus split plus merge keeps reuse high, but a free hole only helps if it is big enough. Watch the gap between total free and the largest free block, not just the totals.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
md: Count distinct 32-byte sectors per warp request. 4 for 32 consecutive floats is ideal; 32 is the worst case and wastes 87.5% of the traffic.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Reading the Speed Of Light rows
md: Speed Of Light does not tell you what to fix. It tells you which of four investigations to open, and whether the kernel has any headroom at all.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Cooperating inside a block: shared memory, barriers and clusters
md: `__syncthreads()` may appear in conditional code only if the condition evaluates the same way for every thread in the block. Otherwise execution may hang or produce unintended side effects. Hoist the barrier out of the branch.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
md: Global search is not cheap per query. The docs call it resource-intensive: the map step makes one LLM call per batch of reports, so lower (more detailed) levels cost more calls. Picking the community level is a quality versus cost dial.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Why PPO is costly for LLMs and what GRPO removes
md: GRPO removes the **critic**, not the reward. In DeepSeekMath, GRPO was trained against a learned reward model. Rule-based verifiable rewards came to the fore with DeepSeek-R1. GRPO and RLVR are separate ideas that work well together.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
md: Do not propagate across trips by default. A bus 15 minutes late on T1 may or may not start its next trip late, depending on the layover. The spec encourages producers to publish TripUpdates for the next trips the same vehicle will run (its block, from block_id in trips.txt) when they are confident, precisely so consumers do not have to guess.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: These are load counts, not latencies. CPUs keep paging-structure caches and multiple TLB levels with model-specific sizes, so a real miss usually skips some loads. The ratios show the direction of the effect; only a measurement on your hardware gives the size.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: The hybrid bet: SSM or linear-attention layers do most of the sequence mixing cheaply, and a handful of full attention layers act as an exact lookup into the past. The Mamba-2 authors put it as SSM layers being a general sequence-to-sequence map while attention layers are "a retrieval mechanism to quickly refer to previous tokens".

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: A cross-encoder reranks the fused shortlist
md: Fusion is about **recall of the shortlist**; reranking is about **precision at the top**. Fused-list quality caps what the reranker can achieve, and rerank depth N trades latency for the chance to rescue documents fused low.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu always returns a threshold, even when nothing changed. On a pair with pure noise it will happily split the noise into two classes and flag a large fraction of the image. Check for a clear gap (or a minimum difference between class means) before trusting the mask.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows
md: Size the **CQ** for the maximum number of completions that can be outstanding (including several per request for multishot operations), not the SQ. Use `IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE` with `cq_entries`, and reap promptly.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
md: Choose by the hard constraint. Many threads and a tight memory budget favour per-CPU caching (tcmalloc). Heavy cross-thread freeing and allocation-heavy runtimes suit mimalloc's per-page lists. Fine-grained control over arenas, decay and introspection (`mallctl`, stats) is jemalloc's strength. Then tune the return-to-OS delay against page-fault cost.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
md: A configuration is only ever best **for a shape on a device**. That is why the tuning result has to be stored under a key that contains the shape, and why `triton.autotune` takes `key=['M', 'N', 'K']`: the docs say a change in those values triggers evaluation of all provided configs.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Scaling across cores: one queue per core, rings and mempools
md: Scaling rule for bypass stacks: **one queue, one owner**. Hardware queues give each core a private path to the device, mempool caches give it private buffers, and rings or messages are the only places cores meet, always in bursts.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
md: A fusion is worth it when it removes HBM round trips or launches without blowing the on-chip budget or recomputing expensive work. Compilers estimate bytes saved, check legality, and fuse greedily; in training they also choose between saving and recomputing activations.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: Distillation trades extra training compute (running a teacher) for a cheaper model to serve. It works best when the student can realistically imitate the teacher; when the gap is large, shrink it with an assistant or an easier teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: FP8 without calibration uses a scale of 1.0. That works when values fit FP8's range, but calibrated scales are what vLLM recommends for best accuracy, and some layers (such as sliding-window ones) can be kept in the native dtype.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving
md: Overlap turns load plus compute into roughly max(load, compute). It is free speed when the two are balanced and nearly useless when one dominates.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Vector clocks: detecting concurrency exactly
md: Lamport clocks give one-way causality in one integer. Vector clocks give exact causality and detect concurrency, at the cost of one integer per node in every timestamp and every message.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
md: Cheap approximate scores filter, exact scores decide. PLAID is the same funnel as BM25 followed by a cross-encoder, built inside one model: centroid ids are the cheap representation and decompressed vectors are the precise one.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: BFS-like (breadth-first-search-like) is an interpretation from probing, not a built-in algorithm. Coconut was never trained to search, keeps no explicit visited set, and the parallelism narrows after a couple of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Always handle the case where the search lands on the edge of the window. With stored min/max bounds, a hit on the boundary is the signal that a non-monotonic model may have pushed the true answer outside.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: SPLADE v2, SPLADE++ and running it in production
md: Do not read the tokens as an explanation. Elastic's docs warn that expansion terms are learned associations, not synonyms, and that low-weight tokens carry information jointly, much like dimensions of a dense vector. A surprising token in a result is not by itself a bug.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is one function with two schedules: a **parallel form** $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$ that is matmul-friendly for training, and a **recurrent form** $S_t=S_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$, $o_t=S_tq_t$ with constant time and memory per generated token.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Measuring judge agreement: confusion matrix and Cohen's kappa
md: Always say which agreement number you report. UMBRELA's GPT-4o labels on TREC DL 2019 to 2023 had 4-grade kappa 0.31 to 0.37 but binarised kappa 0.42 to 0.50 on the same labels. A paper quoting one and a dashboard quoting the other are not comparable.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Designing human evaluations and measuring agreement
md: Do not report raw percent agreement alone. With skewed labels (say 90% of pairs are ties) two annotators agree often by chance. Report kappa with the confusion matrix, and say how ties were handled.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: The scheduler's unit of work is a step with a token budget, not a request. Requests enter and leave between steps, and every step is a fresh decision about who gets how many tokens.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a prompt: rules, delimited inputs and the task
md: A good prompt separates three things the model must not confuse: the rules (stable), the input data (fenced in tags), and the task (stated plainly, ideally last). Then measure: every vendor guide says prompting is iterative and should be checked against test cases.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: From extracted strings to canonical IDs and a bool query
md: The `minimum_should_match` default depends on context. In Elasticsearch it is 1 only when the bool has `should` clauses and no `must` or `filter` clauses; otherwise it is 0, and the should clauses become optional score boosts. Put Berlin and remote as bare should clauses next to a filter list and *every* city passes.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
md: Output tokens are the expensive kind for latency. Prefer designs whose answer is one token or one logit: pointwise labels, PRP in scoring mode, or FIRST-style first-token ranking.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
md: Pick the formulation by its failure mode: pointwise needs calibration, pairwise needs many calls, listwise needs a long context and a good initial order. Most practical gains come from controlling those failure modes (swapping, shuffling, cascades, distillation), not from a cleverer single prompt.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Float descriptors (SIFT) are compared with L2 distance; binary descriptors (ORB) with Hamming distance. Binary descriptors trade some distinctiveness for much cheaper extraction, storage and comparison.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: Garbage collection does not make ABA go away in general. Michael points out that if a program moves the same node back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a stale CAS can still succeed even with perfect GC. What GC (and the schemes in lesson 6) do prevent is the special case where ABA comes from *freeing and reusing* a node someone still references.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
md: Vocabulary trap. "Parsing accuracy" in the 2019 benchmark means grouping, not token-level correctness. Modern papers reserve **PA** for the stricter message-level metric where every static token *and* every parameter must be identified correctly, and use **GA** for grouping. A number quoted without its metric is worthless, so always ask: grouping or tokens, per message or per template?

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Uniform interpolation protects the slow pairs but blurs the fast ones. Every better method since PI is about treating pairs differently according to their wavelength.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: Looping saves **parameters** (memory, communication), not **compute**. Every loop is another full pass through the block, and the passes are sequential, so a $(1 \otimes 12)$ model is about as slow per token as a 12-layer model. Looped models trade memory for depth, they do not make inference free.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: A d90 of 200 does not mean that 200 hand-picked weights would do. The 200 numbers are projected through a dense random map, so every original weight still moves a little. And 90% of full performance is the bar, not 100%.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Approximate unlearning: gradient ascent, collapse and NPO
md: "Loss on the forget set went up" is not evidence of good unlearning. GA can drive that loss arbitrarily high by wrecking the model. Always read forget metrics next to utility metrics and next to the retrained reference.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Truncate, then re-normalize: the mechanics on a toy vector
md: Re-normalizing the query alone never changes a ranking: it scales every score by the same number. What changes rankings is the documents' prefix lengths, so re-normalize the stored document prefixes (or compute true cosine). OpenAI's embedding guide says the same: if you shorten vectors yourself, normalize them.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: The 5as/h term assumes attention materializes the s x s score matrix. Fused attention kernels (FlashAttention style, as in Transformer Engine) never store it, so most of that term disappears by itself. Megatron Core's config even warns that with fused attention there is no need to put core_attn in --recompute-modules.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging
md: Setting `dirty_decay_ms` to 0 is not a free fix. The manual says it purges dirty pages immediately when they are created, so every page that empties pays for a purge, and every later reuse pays a page fault. It lowers RSS that is merely waiting; it does nothing for pages pinned by live objects.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: `volatile` is not an ordering. In standard C++, volatile accesses are not atomic and do not order other memory, so they cannot be used for synchronization between threads. (MSVC gives volatile acquire/release semantics by default on x86 targets; that is a compiler extension, not the language.)

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Do not benchmark a reclamation scheme with one thread on an idle machine. The cost differences that matter, garbage growth under preemption and fence cost on long traversals, only appear with oversubscribed threads, update-heavy workloads and long data structures.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: ArcFace: putting an angular margin inside a classifier
md: The class weights only cover training identities. At test time you discard them and compare normalized features with cosine similarity, exactly as with a triplet-trained model. A large classification accuracy on training classes is not the goal.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Misconception: "disabling ASLR and pinning the CPU makes my benchmark correct". They reduce run-to-run noise, which narrows intervals. A narrow interval around a biased setup is a confidently wrong answer.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
md: The Miles fault-tolerance page is marked **outdated**: it describes the pre-refactor stack, and new machinery is still being merged. Also note that P2P writes are bounded by `--p2p-transfer-timeout` (default 30 s) and a failed write fails the update; the docs state there is no automatic retry or fallback to broadcast.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Reported speedups are relative to specific baselines on specific traces: B-LRU on six CDN traces, a tuned weighted fair scheduler on TPC-H mixes, a read-optimized B-tree on read-only integer keys. A different workload, or a stronger baseline, can shrink the gain to zero.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Unmerged does not mean easy. Requests in one batch use adapters with different ranks and different sequence lengths, so padding everything into one batched matmul wastes work. S-LoRA's variant that copies adapters into contiguous memory and uses padded batched matmul (S-LoRA-bmm) was much slower than the version with custom kernels.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: RRF rewards agreement between phrasings. A relevant document that only one phrasing finds stays low, and a junk document that two phrasings share can outrank it. That is why the quality of the phrasings matters as much as their number.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Common misconception: an MTP model does not have to emit several tokens per step. Gloeckle et al. use only the next-token head for ordinary decoding. The other heads are optional, and lesson 5 shows how they can be reused to draft tokens for faster decoding.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Shampoo: one preconditioner for the rows, one for the columns
md: A frequent mistake is to read $L^{-1/4}$ as an elementwise power. It is a *matrix* power: eigendecompose $L = Q \Lambda Q^\top$ and take $Q \Lambda^{-1/4} Q^\top$. That needs float32 (or better) and an eigensolver, which is why roots are only refreshed every $f$ steps.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
md: Common misconception: "SP is broken only because the learning rate is too large for big models." Lowering it uniformly fixes the exploding layers but freezes others, such as the input embeddings. The issue is the *relative* scaling between layers.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
md: FUTEX_WAIT says "sleep only if the word still holds the value I based my decision on". That expected-value check, done atomically by the kernel, is what makes lost wake-ups impossible.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
md: Read Committed is not a weaker form of a single consistent view. Each statement sees one snapshot, but an updating statement can also see newer versions of the rows it is about to change, so a single UPDATE or DELETE can mix two moments in time. The docs call it unsuitable for commands with complex search conditions.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: BIO, IOB1 and BIOES: tag sets that make spans decodable
md: The repair rule is not cosmetic: it changes your score. [seqeval](https://github.com/chakki-works/seqeval) documents that for gold `B-NP I-NP O` and prediction `I-NP I-NP O`, its default mode (which mimics the conlleval Perl script) gives precision, recall and F1 of 1.00, while `mode='strict'` with `scheme=IOB2` gives 0.00. Same predictions, two different papers' worth of difference. Always say which mode you used.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens
md: Neither NSA nor DSA shrinks the KV cache. NSA adds compressed and per-branch keys; DSA adds an indexer key per token. Both cut the bytes *read and computed* per query. Also, DSA's indexer is still $O(L^2)$ over a sequence, just with a much smaller constant.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
md: The single controller does not mean all tensors flow through one process. Large transfers, especially weight refit, go over channels the controller sets up (CUDA IPC or NCCL), not through the controller itself.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Setting a policy does not move pages that already exist. `mbind(2)` affects only new allocations unless you pass `MPOL_MF_MOVE` (or `MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL`, which needs CAP_SYS_NICE). Install the policy before the first touch, or ask for migration explicitly.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
md: NVMe queue depth does not make flash faster; it lets the controller keep many dies busy. One synchronous 4 KB read at a time pays the full read latency per request no matter how many queues the drive has. Use async I/O (io_uring, SPDK, or many threads) to keep enough requests in flight.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: A density map gives a number, not a list of objects. You cannot crop, identify or follow an individual from it, and the count is real-valued. Use it when objects are too dense to box, not as a default.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
md: A common misconception: "we log everything, so we are observable". Logs scale with traffic times fields per event, metrics scale with the number of distinct label combinations, and traces scale with the sampling rate. Choosing where each fact lives is the design work.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: A common bug: cropping a single field, such as a price, and running Tesseract with the default `--psm 3`. Automatic page segmentation expects a page and can find no lines at all in a tight crop. Use `--psm 7` (one line) or `--psm 8` (one word), and leave a small white border around the text.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
md: ANLS cannot tell a harmless typo from a costly one: `42.50` predicted as `42.5` scores 0.8, the same as many genuine digit errors of similar size. For money and IDs, add field-level exact match after normalization.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: CI is a contract written in the repo: on these events, on these machines, run these commands, and block the merge unless they exit with status 0. Read `.github/workflows/` before your first PR to a project.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Misconception: a reviewer who leaves 15 comments is blocking you on all 15. Often most are optional. If the reviewer did not say which ones block the merge, ask instead of guessing.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: Read in this order before you touch code: LICENSE (can you contribute at all), CONTRIBUTING (how), CODE_OF_CONDUCT (how to behave), SECURITY (if your finding is a vulnerability). Ten minutes of reading avoids a rejected PR.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebase rewrites history. Pro Git's rule: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on. Your own PR branch is the usual exception, which is why the next lesson's force-push needs care, not a ban.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: Public is not the same as open source. Code you can read on GitHub with no license file is all rights reserved, and so is a snippet whose license you never checked.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: CLA: one signed agreement per person or company, granting rights up front. DCO: no agreement, just a per-commit certification of origin via Signed-off-by, checked mechanically by email match.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
md: A common mistake is to fix a bug inside a generated file. Your edit is overwritten the next time the generator runs, and reviewers will reject it. When a file says *do not edit*, find its input (here `src/commands/get.json`) in the build rule and change that instead.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: Every cut is an experiment: remove, rerun, compare to the original failure. Keep cuts that preserve the exact error; undo the rest.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: If the project squash-merges PRs, your intermediate commits disappear from the main branch anyway, and the PR as a whole becomes one commit. That makes **one logical change per PR** even more important: the squash cannot separate a fix from a speedup after the fact.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: The block table is the whole trick: contiguous logical blocks, scattered physical blocks, allocation on demand. Waste is capped at one partly filled block per sequence.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call
md: Raising the frequency is not free. Every sample means an interrupt, a stack walk and a record written to disk. Gregg suggests going up toward 997 Hz only when you need finer resolution, for example to catch short bursts.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Common misconception: "unflushed stores are lost on a crash." Some are, some are not, and the hardware chooses. Treat each dirty cache line as independently maybe-persisted. Flushes give you a lower bound on what is durable, never an upper bound.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
md: C keeps your field order and you are responsible for packing it well. Rust's default repr may reorder fields and use niches to save space, but promises no exact layout. Use `#[repr(C)]` whenever bytes cross a boundary your compiler does not control.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: The independence assumption is the optimistic case. If the filter is anti-correlated with the query (the nearest vectors to *winter coats* are rarely in *city = Miami*), the survivors sit even deeper in the ranking. The ACORN paper notes post-filtering's expected cost is about $\log n + k/s$ (k results wanted) for uniformly spread matches but degrades toward $O(n)$ when matching vectors are far from the query.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight
md: **Prefetching is a way to raise concurrency.** A prefetch is a miss started early, before the program's own load. Anything that lets more independent misses overlap (prefetchers, unrolled loops, several independent lists walked at once, more threads) moves you up the curve.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
md: Same scores, three uses: rerank finished solutions (weighted voting is a strong default), prune partial solutions in beam search (best on harder problems at modest budgets), or provide step-level rewards so RL can credit each step separately.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: The one number to remember is not the microseconds of a single switch but **switches per second times total cost per switch**, where total includes the cache and TLB refill. Keep CPU-bound threads near the core count, and reserve extra threads or async I/O for work that actually waits.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Worked example: selecting a prompt and the winner's curse
md: The data that chose the prompt cannot also grade it. Report the selected prompt's score on a held-out set that played no part in any choice, and expect it to be lower than the dev score.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Vocabulary mismatch: why BM25 misses relevant documents
md: Better scoring cannot fix a zero-overlap miss. Query expansion changes **which documents can match at all** by adding terms to the query (or, in document expansion, to the documents). That is a recall tool first, and every added term is also a new way to match the wrong document.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Paying for it: latency, cost and when not to rewrite
md: Misconception: rewriting is free accuracy. Besides latency and cost, a rewriter can **drift** from the user's intent (RAG-Fusion's evaluation saw off-topic answers from unrelated generated queries) and it is a new failure point (timeouts, malformed output). Keep the original query as a fallback or as one of the queries, and log every rewrite next to the original so you can audit drift.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Paxos: choosing one value with prepare and accept
md: A Paxos proposer is not free to pick its value. After phase 1 it must adopt the value of the highest-numbered proposal any acceptor in its majority reports. That single rule is what keeps a chosen value from ever changing.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Prompting the generator to answer with citations
md: A citation is a claim, not a proof. The model can attach [3] to a sentence [3] does not support, as it did here. ALCE found even the best models lacked complete citation support about 50% of the time on ELI5, so check citations automatically rather than trusting their presence.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve
md: Features used for training must be produced by the same code, against the same index state and at the same moment as the features used for serving. Log the vector at query time; do not reconstruct it later.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Queue pairs, work requests and the completion queue
md: The rdma-core man page is explicit: buffers used by a WR may only be reused after the request completes and its completion has been polled. The one exception is `IBV_SEND_INLINE` (SEND and RDMA WRITE only), which copies the payload into the WQE itself, so the buffer is reusable as soon as `ibv_post_send` returns.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Client-side prediction and server reconciliation
md: Reconciliation does not prevent all corrections. With a single player and a deterministic simulation the replay always matches; with other players acting at the same time the server can legitimately disagree. Games usually smooth the correction over a few frames rather than snapping.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
md: Do not drop the zeros. Training only on observed implicit events (all with p = 1) lets the model predict 1 everywhere and still reach zero loss. The low-confidence zeros are what make the scores discriminative.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo
md: A common misconception is that the pixels-per-mm method only fails at extreme angles. In this toy, a moderate 40 degree tilt already puts it 15 percent off. Under perspective, scale varies with both position and direction across the plane.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The planner is only as good as its row estimates. It searches join orders exhaustively by dynamic programming up to a limit, then genetically; but a 100x row misestimate can turn the cheapest-looking plan into the slowest. Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE estimates against actuals first.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: A precise test: when is a proxy unhackable?
md: Unhackability is a very strong condition. For rich policy classes, every proxy that is not simply equivalent to the true reward (same ranking of all policies) can be hacked by some policy. Skalse et al. conclude that learned rewards are better treated as aids to policy learning than as specifications to optimize without limit. The practical question becomes how far you can optimize before hacking appears.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Colocated or disaggregated: where the engines live
md: Colocation trades memory and switch time for zero idle pools. Disaggregation trades network sync and staleness for overlap and freedom to size each pool. The long tail pushes large reasoning runs toward disaggregated, asynchronous designs.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Ceilings, hierarchical rooflines and Nsight Compute
md: Read the gaps. In the NERSC DeepCAM study, a kernel whose L1, L2 and HBM points sit close together shows a streaming pattern with poor cache locality; a large gap between the L2 and HBM points shows that L2 misses were rare. The binding level is the one whose roof is lowest at that level's own intensity.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: At the default k = 60 with typical windows (tens of results), RRF behaves like a vote count first (how many lists returned the document) and uses ranks mainly to order documents with the same count. Smaller k gives ranks more say; larger k makes it closer to pure vote counting.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: From -ENOMEM and ERR_PTR to Result
md: `to_result` is not a general converter. For a C function that returns a byte count or an index on success, use the raw value: check `< 0` yourself or write a small wrapper that returns `Result<usize>`. Otherwise the success value silently disappears.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Stashing a task in a BPF map from `select_cpu` does not skip `enqueue`; only a DSQ insertion does. The docs call storing tasks from `select_cpu` racy and discouraged. Also, the core ignores an invalid CPU choice such as one outside the task's allowed cpumask.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
md: A self-improvement loop is only as good as its filter. The precision of the check sets the quality of the kept data, and the set of problems the model can sometimes solve sets how far the loop can reach.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Compression has costs of its own. The compressor runs on the critical path of every request. The compressed text is hard for humans to read, which makes debugging and audits harder. Exact strings (code, JSON, numbers, IDs) can be damaged by token deletion. And question-aware compression produces a different context for every question, so that context can no longer be served from the provider's prefix cache.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
md: Cache locality and load balance pull against each other. Sending every request of a hot prefix to one worker maximizes hits and can overload that worker; the balance thresholds exist to break locality when queues diverge. The gateway's trees are approximate: they are inferred from routed text, not read from the workers, so they can be stale.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: No technique wins on every axis. Look at query time, preprocessing time, memory, how quickly new traffic weights can be applied, and whether turns and other metrics are supported. A static fastest-route server and a live-traffic service often choose differently.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
md: Every hand-written SIMD loop has a vector body, a horizontal reduction and a tail. A vector reduction adds in a different order than the scalar loop, so float results can change, which is why compilers need permission to reassociate.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: "Arena" means different things in different allocators. In this lesson it is a bump region freed all at once. In jemalloc (and glibc malloc) an *arena* is an independent general-purpose heap with its own locks, used so threads contend less; you still free objects one by one there.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: "Disaggregated" here is about trainer versus rollout GPUs. It is unrelated to PD disaggregation (`--prefill-num-servers`), which splits SGLang's own prefill and decode work, and it does not imply async training by itself.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: Words to keep apart: a **latent** is a unit of the SAE; a **feature** is the concept you hope it captures. Gemma Scope says 'latents' for exactly this reason. A latent with a clean name is a hypothesis about a model feature, not proof of one.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Interpolation is not the same as smoothing. Most of these methods are *exact*: the surface passes through every reading. That is right for precise instruments and wrong for noisy cheap sensors, where you want a method that can treat part of each reading as measurement error.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Choose interpolators by held-out error, not by reputation. Leave-one-out RMSE (or blocked cross-validation) compares methods on your data, and the standardized errors tell you whether kriging's uncertainty can be trusted.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
md: A log-mel spectrogram is 80 numbers every 10 ms. Whisper's 30 second input is therefore an 80 x 3000 matrix: the model never sees raw samples.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: Stack memory lives exactly as long as the function call that created it. Allocation and release are a pointer adjustment, which is why the size must be bounded and why anything that must outlive the call has to go somewhere else: the heap.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
md: Most page faults are normal: they are how Linux allocates memory on first touch and copies pages only on write. Count them with getrusage or `perf`; worry about major faults and fault storms, not their existence.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
md: Kafka turns backpressure from data loss into delay: as long as retention covers the backlog, a slow consumer only falls behind. The bounded buffers inside the processor are what make the slowdown propagate instead of growing memory without bound.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
md: Scaling by the square root of d_k is not mainly about float overflow (implementations subtract the row max before exponentiating anyway). It keeps softmax out of its saturated, near one-hot region so gradients stay usable as d_k grows.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
md: Saturation does not mean repeated terms are ignored. With k1 = 1.2, going from 1 to 2 occurrences still raises the factor from 0.45 to 0.62. It means each extra occurrence is worth less than the one before, with a hard ceiling.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
md: Pre-LN vs post-LN is not cosmetic. Xiong et al. show that in the original post-LN Transformer the gradients near the output are large at initialization, which is why it needs a careful learning-rate warmup. Placing LayerNorm inside the residual branch, as GPT-2 does, gives well-behaved gradients at initialization.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
md: A common slip is evaluating the outer derivative at $x$ instead of at the inner value. Here $f'(u) = 2u$ must use $u = 7$, giving 14, not $2 \times 2 = 4$. That is why the forward values are computed and stored first: the backward step needs them.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
md: Do not test your quoting in zsh and assume bash agrees. zsh, the default interactive shell on macOS, does **not** word-split unquoted parameter expansions unless the `SH_WORD_SPLIT` option is set. Scripts that start with `#!/bin/bash` or `#!/bin/sh` follow the splitting rules shown here.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
md: Skip-gram is not trained to be a good language model; the prediction task is a pretext. Mikolov et al. say plainly that the skip-gram model is only concerned with learning high-quality vector representations. After training, the output layer is usually thrown away and the input vectors are kept as the embeddings.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Doubling peak TFLOP/s does almost nothing for batch-1 decode. What helps is moving fewer bytes per token (smaller or quantized weights, which for example halve the bytes at 8 bits) or using each byte for more tokens (batching, next lessons).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
md: Simplified: real CPUs pipeline and overlap many instructions, and even execute them out of order. But they are built so that the visible result is exactly as if each instruction ran one at a time in program order, which is why this model is the right one to reason with.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
md: A low pretraining loss does not mean a helpful model. The loss rewards matching the *distribution* of internet text, including its errors, rudeness and rambling. That is exactly why the later stages exist.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
md: An inverted index alone does not rank anything. Boolean retrieval returns an unordered set: a document either matches or it does not. Ranking needs term weights, which lessons 4 and 5 add on top of the same postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
md: TF-IDF still has two flaws that cosine only partly fixes: tf keeps growing with every repetition (keyword stuffing pays), and length normalization is crude. BM25, the next course, keeps the same inverted index and replaces the weighting with a saturating tf and a tunable length normalization.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Before you keep a pointer, ask how long the object behind it lives. Locals die when their function returns, malloc'd memory dies at free, and realloc can retire the old address at any call.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: The rule is not "only one reference to a variable per function". Sequential borrows are fine, as are many shared ones. The error only appears when a `&mut` borrow overlaps any other live borrow of the same value.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: Not every useful function is linear. $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \ne 0$ is **affine**: it moves the origin, so $f(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{b}$ instead of $\mathbf{0}$. Neural network layers are affine, and their activation functions (like ReLU) are not linear at all. That nonlinearity is what lets a deep network do more than one big matrix could.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: stepping downhill, and how big a step
md: Gradient descent: $w \leftarrow w - \eta \nabla L$. On a quadratic, each step multiplies the error by $1 - \eta\lambda$ per direction, so it converges only if $\eta < 2/\lambda$ for every curvature $\lambda$, and the sharpest direction sets the limit.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies
md: Keep the cached values. The forward pass is not just for the prediction: the backward pass will reuse every $z^l$ and $a^l$ computed here, so frameworks store them.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
md: Any read-modify-write of shared data (even `x++`) is several instructions, and a context switch can split them. Protect every critical section with a lock, and build locks on atomic hardware instructions, never on plain loads and stores.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
md: Linearity of expectation needs no independence, but the variance addition rule does. For dependent variables, $\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$, where the **covariance** measures how they move together.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: $C \approx 6ND$. For a fixed budget, parameters and tokens trade off one for one in ratio: double $N$ and you must halve $D$.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
md: A common bug: dividing by the number of relevant documents *retrieved* (4) instead of all relevant documents (5). That gives 0.642 instead of 0.513 and silently rewards systems that retrieve fewer relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: In-batch negatives assume the other passages are wrong. If the batch holds two copies of the same passage, or two paraphrased questions, the loss pushes a correct answer away. sentence-transformers recommends the `NO_DUPLICATES` batch sampler for this reason. Hard negatives mined automatically can also be unlabeled positives, so they need filtering.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
md: Encoding is **not** "find the longest matching token from the left" and not "pick the segmentation with fewest tokens". BPE applies merges greedily in the order they were learned. A different procedure over the same vocabulary can give a different split, and the model was trained on BPE's split.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: A debugging recipe: loss at init, overfit one batch, read the curves
md: Every check has a **known right answer**: loss at init equals $\ln C$, one batch overfits to about zero, the real model beats an input-independent baseline. Add one piece of complexity at a time and re-check, so when something breaks you know which change did it.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Why resampling your own outputs erases rare events
md: Model collapse is not caused by a bad model or a bug. In this example fitting is exact. The finite sample alone, which Shumailov et al. call **statistical approximation error**, is enough to drive the process.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: vdso(7) states that calls served by the vDSO do not appear in `strace` output and are invisible to seccomp filters. A trace with zero `clock_gettime` lines does not mean the program never asks for the time.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Coordinated omission: the load tester stops looking when it hurts
md: Coordinated omission does not make individual samples wrong: the 2 ms readings were real. The bug is which samples exist. The tester samples less often precisely when the server is slow, so the sample set is biased toward good moments. No statistic computed afterwards can recover samples that were never taken.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
md: Every time-scoped question becomes interval arithmetic once two things are fixed: the reference date, and the convention for partial dates. Allen relations, current-role tests and window clipping are all a few endpoint comparisons.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: The best use of test-time compute depends on the prompt. Search is most valuable where the model is weak but not hopeless; on easy prompts it can hurt by exploiting the verifier.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
md: Titans' memory update = gradient descent with momentum (carry surprise forward) and weight decay (forget), all gated per token. Momentum keeps writing after a surprising event; forgetting keeps a fixed-size memory from overflowing.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers
md: Tiering wins only if the *hot* pages live in the fast tier. The capacity of each tier matters less than the fraction of accesses it serves. Everything in this course is machinery for keeping $h$ high cheaply.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Naive, seasonal naive and simple exponential smoothing
md: A parameter fitted to minimize one-step in-sample error is not automatically good at the horizon you care about. Always evaluate at the real horizon on data the fit never saw.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
md: Autotuning has costs you do not see in steady state: the first call for each new `key` value compiles and benchmarks every config, and each distinct constexpr combination is a separate compiled kernel. Keep `key` to arguments that really change the best config, and use `prune_configs_by` to drop hopeless candidates.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
md: No axis is free. Discrete plus causal is the simplest to train and serve; continuous plus bidirectional plus separate encoders has led the reported GenEval numbers in these papers, at the cost of more moving parts.
